entries.meaning: Of the Pacific Ocean or the lands around it. ---
examples: We drove up the Pacific coast from San Diego.
Pacific storms hit Oregon first.
She studies Pacific island languages.
entries.contrast: With a capital it means the ocean. Lowercase pacific is a formal word for peaceful (a pacific gesture), and it is rare in speech.

entries.meaning: Opposed to war and to violence on principle. ---
examples: He came from a pacifist family.
Pacifist groups organized the march.
Her politics are firmly pacifist.
entries.contrast: Much more often a noun: She's a pacifist. As an adjective it describes beliefs, families and movements.

entries.meaning: Packaged has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Packaged foods list the salt on the side of the box.
We buy packaged rice because it keeps longer.
They booked a packaged tour of Italy.
It's a packaged deal: hotel, car and flights.

senses.head: Sold in a box, bag or wrapper rather than loose
examples: Packaged foods list the salt on the side of the box.
We buy packaged rice because it keeps longer.

senses.head: Sold as one deal with everything included
examples: They booked a packaged tour of Italy.
It's a packaged deal: hotel, car and flights.

entries.meaning: Padded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She sat on a padded bench by the window.
The jacket is padded at the shoulders.
The bill was padded with fees nobody explained.
He turned in a padded resume and got caught.

senses.head: With soft material inside for comfort or protection
examples: She sat on a padded bench by the window.
The jacket is padded at the shoulders.

senses.head: Made bigger by adding things that do not belong there
examples: The bill was padded with fees nobody explained.
He turned in a padded resume and got caught.

entries.русский: мягкий, с подкладкой; раздутый (о счёте, резюме)

entries.meaning: Belonging to an old religion that came before Christianity, or to modern nature worship. ---
examples: Many Christmas customs have pagan roots.
The museum has a room of pagan statues.
Her grandmother called the festival pagan and refused to go.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (the pagans of northern Europe). Capitalized Pagan usually means the living modern religion; lowercase points to the pre-Christian world.

entries.meaning: Paid has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She took a paid internship in Denver.
We get ten days of paid leave a year.
The invoice is paid in full.
Mark the account paid and file it.

senses.head: That you receive money for
examples: She took a paid internship in Denver.
We get ten days of paid leave a year.

senses.head: Already settled, of a bill or an account
examples: The invoice is paid in full.
Mark the account paid and file it.

entries.comparison: not gradable — but compounds compare: better paid, the best-paid job in town

entries.meaning: Feeling no pain, or causing none. ---
examples: Two weeks after surgery she was finally pain-free.
They advertise a pain-free dental visit.
No treatment is completely pain-free.

entries.meaning: Showing that you are hurt, upset or embarrassed. ---
examples: He gave me a pained smile and changed the subject.
There was a pained silence after the question.
She looked pained when I mentioned his name.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a pained expression
entries.contrast: Pained shows hurt feelings on a face; painful causes pain. A pained smile hurts nobody; a painful shot does.

entries.meaning: Painful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The shot was quick but painful.
He has a painful knee and won't see anyone about it.
It was a painful conversation for both of them.
Losing that game was more painful than the whole season.

senses.head: Hurting the body
examples: The shot was quick but painful.
He has a painful knee and won't see anyone about it.

senses.head: Hard to go through, to remember or to watch
examples: It was a painful conversation for both of them.
Losing that game was more painful than the whole season.

entries.contrast: A thing that hurts you is painful; a face that shows hurt is pained.

entries.meaning: Painless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The procedure is quick and painless.
They promised a painless shot, and it was.
Moving the files over was painless.
There is no painless way to fire someone.

senses.head: Causing no physical pain
examples: The procedure is quick and painless.
They promised a painless shot, and it was.

senses.head: Easy, with no trouble or effort
examples: Moving the files over was painless.
There is no painless way to fire someone.

entries.meaning: Done slowly and with great care for every detail. ---
examples: The restoration was slow, painstaking work.
She kept painstaking notes of every call.
It took painstaking research to find the name.
entries.position: both — almost always before a noun

entries.meaning: Covered or decorated with paint. ---
examples: The painted door was still sticky.
She bought a hand-painted bowl in Oaxaca.
The walls are painted a soft gray.

entries.meaning: Of or from Pakistan, its people or its culture. ---
examples: We went to a Pakistani restaurant on Devon Avenue.
Her parents are Pakistani.
Pakistani mangoes reach the stores in June.
entries.position: both — a Pakistani restaurant, Her parents are Pakistani
entries.contrast: Also a noun (two Pakistanis), but a Pakistani woman is the safer wording for a person.

entries.meaning: Palatable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The soup was bland but palatable.
A little lemon makes it more palatable.
They rewrote the bill to make it palatable to both parties.
By then there was no palatable option left.

senses.head: Good enough to eat or drink
examples: The soup was bland but palatable.
A little lemon makes it more palatable.

senses.head: Acceptable to people, of an idea or a decision
examples: They rewrote the bill to make it palatable to both parties.
By then there was no palatable option left.

entries.meaning: Very large and grand, like a palace. ---
examples: They rented a palatial house on the lake.
The lobby is palatial, all marble and gold.
It's the most palatial hotel in the state.

entries.meaning: Of the earliest and longest part of the Stone Age. ---
examples: The cave holds Paleolithic paintings.
Paleolithic tools were chipped, not polished.
He teaches a course on Paleolithic Europe.
entries.contrast: American spelling Paleolithic; British books print Palaeolithic.

entries.meaning: Of or from Palestine, or of the Palestinian people. ---
examples: A Palestinian poet read at the festival.
Her mother is Palestinian.
Palestinian families have lived in the camp for decades.

entries.meaning: Easing pain or symptoms without curing the cause. ---
examples: She moved into palliative care in the spring.
The drug is palliative, not a cure.
They offered only palliative measures.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: palliative care
entries.contrast: Also a noun (a palliative). Palliative care eases symptoms; it does not try to cure the disease.

entries.meaning: Palpable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The tension in the room was palpable.
There was a palpable sense of relief when he walked in.
The lump was palpable on the left side.
The doctor found no palpable swelling.

senses.head: So strong that you can almost touch it, of a feeling in a room
examples: The tension in the room was palpable.
There was a palpable sense of relief when he walked in.

senses.head: In medicine: that a doctor can feel with the hands
examples: The lump was palpable on the left side.
The doctor found no palpable swelling.

entries.meaning: Embarrassingly small, of an amount or an offer. ---
examples: They offered a paltry two percent raise.
He sold the painting for a paltry sum.
The second offer was even paltrier than the first.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a paltry sum

entries.meaning: Of or from Panama. ---
examples: A Panamanian crew ran the boat.
His wife is Panamanian.
Panamanian coffee is hard to find here.

entries.meaning: Of the pancreas. ---
examples: Pancreatic cancer is hard to catch early.
The scan showed a pancreatic cyst.
He takes pancreatic enzymes with every meal.

entries.meaning: Of a disease that has spread across many countries. ---
examples: Pandemic flu spreads faster than the seasonal kind.
The virus reached pandemic levels in three months.
Officials still describe the outbreak as pandemic.
entries.contrast: These days far more often a noun: during the pandemic. An epidemic stays in one region; a pandemic crosses countries.

entries.meaning: Covered with flat boards of wood on the walls. ---
examples: He works in a dark, paneled study.
The walls are paneled in oak.
They drove a wood-paneled station wagon.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun, and often in compounds: wood-paneled
entries.contrast: American paneled with one l; British books print panelled.

entries.meaning: Suddenly so frightened that you cannot think. ---
examples: Panic-stricken shoppers ran for the doors.
She called me, panic-stricken, at two in the morning.
He was panic-stricken when he couldn't find his passport.

entries.meaning: Filled with sudden fear, or showing it. ---
examples: A panicked crowd pushed toward the exit.
She sent a panicked text about the deadline.
I was too panicked to think straight.
entries.form: -ed from panic — a k is added before the ending
entries.contrast: Watch the spelling: panicked, panicking, both with a k.

entries.meaning: Beginning to panic, or easily made to panic. ---
examples: I get panicky in crowds.
Don't send a panicky email at midnight.
The market turned panicky after the announcement.

entries.meaning: Taking in a wide view in every direction. ---
examples: The room has a panoramic view of the bay.
He took a panoramic photo from the roof.
Panoramic windows run the length of the restaurant.

entries.meaning: Of the pope. ---
examples: The papal visit filled the square.
She quoted a papal letter from 1963.
Papal elections are held behind closed doors.

entries.meaning: True and self-contradictory at the same time. ---
examples: It's paradoxical that the safer car makes people drive faster.
She has a paradoxical love of rules and of breaking them.
The result seems paradoxical until you read the footnote.

entries.meaning: Of or from Paraguay. ---
examples: A Paraguayan harpist opened the concert.
Her husband is Paraguayan.
Paraguayan beef is sold all over the region.

entries.meaning: Parallel has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The street runs parallel to the river.
Draw two parallel lines an inch apart.
The two investigations were parallel but separate.
He led a parallel life in another city.

senses.head: Running side by side, always the same distance apart
examples: The street runs parallel to the river.
Draw two parallel lines an inch apart.

senses.head: Similar and happening at the same time
examples: The two investigations were parallel but separate.
He led a parallel life in another city.

entries.contrast: Watch the spelling: one r, then two ls, then one. It is also a noun (draw a parallel) and a verb (Her story parallels his).

entries.meaning: Paralyzed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was paralyzed from the waist down after the crash.
Her left arm is paralyzed.
I was paralyzed with fear and just stood there.
The strike left the airport paralyzed for two days.

senses.head: Unable to move part or all of the body
examples: He was paralyzed from the waist down after the crash.
Her left arm is paralyzed.

senses.head: Unable to act or to function at all
examples: I was paralyzed with fear and just stood there.
The strike left the airport paralyzed for two days.

entries.contrast: American paralyzed; British books print paralysed.

entries.meaning: Organized and armed like an army, but not part of the official one. ---
examples: A paramilitary group controlled the border.
They wore paramilitary uniforms without insignia.
Paramilitary training camps operated there for years.

entries.meaning: More important than anything else. ---
examples: Safety is paramount on the job site.
The question is of paramount importance.
For her, family is paramount.
entries.position: both — of paramount importance, Safety is paramount

entries.meaning: Wrongly convinced that people are out to harm you, or simply far too suspicious. ---
examples: I'm paranoid about leaving the stove on.
He got paranoid after reading the comments.
She's the most paranoid person I know about passwords.
entries.contrast: In everyday talk it just means far too suspicious (paranoid about locking the door); in medicine it names a serious condition, so it is worth keeping the joking use for small worries.

entries.meaning: Of events that science cannot explain, like ghosts or telepathy. ---
examples: She writes paranormal romance novels.
The show investigates paranormal activity in old hotels.
Nothing about the noise was paranormal — it was the pipes.

entries.meaning: Unable to move the legs and the lower body. ---
examples: He has been paraplegic since the accident.
The center trains paraplegic athletes.
Paraplegic patients relearn how to get around.
entries.contrast: Also a noun, but many people prefer a paraplegic man or a man with paraplegia to a paraplegic.

entries.meaning: Parasitic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Parasitic worms are common in the region.
The plant is parasitic and takes water from the tree.
He called the middlemen parasitic.
It's a parasitic business model and everyone knows it.

senses.head: Living on or inside another living thing and feeding off it
examples: Parasitic worms are common in the region.
The plant is parasitic and takes water from the tree.

senses.head: Living off other people's work or money
examples: He called the middlemen parasitic.
It's a parasitic business model and everyone knows it.

entries.meaning: Parched has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The fields were parched after two months without rain.
My lips were parched from the wind.
I'm parched — is there any water?
After the hike we were all parched.

senses.head: Very dry, of land, lips or a throat
examples: The fields were parched after two months without rain.
My lips were parched from the wind.

senses.head: Informal: very thirsty
examples: I'm parched — is there any water?
After the hike we were all parched.

entries.meaning: Of a parent or of parents. ---
examples: Parental consent is required for the trip.
The app has parental controls.
She took parental leave in March.

entries.meaning: Added as an aside, in brackets or between commas. ---
examples: He added a parenthetical note about the source.
Her parenthetical remark turned out to be the whole point.
The comment was parenthetical and got cut.

entries.meaning: Of or from Paris. ---
examples: We stayed in a tiny Parisian apartment.
Her accent is unmistakably Parisian.
Parisian cafes fill up after six.

entries.meaning: Standing where it was left, of a vehicle. ---
examples: A parked car blocked the driveway.
The truck is parked around the corner.
She hit a parked van backing out.
entries.position: both — before a noun (a parked car); after be it is usually the passive: The car is parked outside

entries.meaning: Of a parliament or of the way one works. ---
examples: Canada has a parliamentary system.
The parliamentary election is set for June.
He knows every parliamentary rule by heart.
entries.contrast: The middle is pronounced pahr-luh-, not pahr-lee-uh-, even though the spelling shows -lia-.

entries.meaning: Parochial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She went to a parochial school in Boston.
Most parochial schools charge tuition.
His view of the country is pretty parochial.
The debate was parochial and missed the larger question.

senses.head: Of a church parish, especially of a parish school
examples: She went to a parochial school in Boston.
Most parochial schools charge tuition.

senses.head: Interested only in your own small corner of the world
examples: His view of the country is pretty parochial.
The debate was parochial and missed the larger question.

entries.meaning: Unwilling to spend or to give, even when there is plenty. ---
examples: The company is parsimonious with raises.
He kept a parsimonious household on a very good salary.
She's more parsimonious than poor.
entries.contrast: Formal and a little bookish. In speech Americans say cheap or stingy.

entries.meaning: Partial has 3 distinct senses.
examples: We got a partial refund.
They have only a partial list of names.
A judge must not be partial.
The report was partial, and everyone in the room knew it.
I'm partial to dark chocolate.
He's partial to old westerns.

senses.head: Not complete
examples: We got a partial refund.
They have only a partial list of names.

senses.head: Favoring one side instead of judging fairly
examples: A judge must not be partial.
The report was partial, and everyone in the room knew it.

senses.head: Fond of something
examples: I'm partial to dark chocolate.
He's partial to old westerns.

entries.comparison: not gradable — except in the third sense: more partial to sweets
entries.takes: to + noun or -ing, in the third sense

entries.meaning: Taking part in a program or an offer, of a business or a school. ---
examples: The offer is good at participating locations only.
Participating pharmacies give the shot for free.
A list of participating schools is on the website.

entries.meaning: Built so that ordinary people take part in the decisions. ---
examples: The city tried participatory budgeting.
It's a participatory museum, and you touch everything.
Participatory democracy takes more time than voting once a year.
entries.русский: основанный на участии, с участием людей

entries.meaning: Partisan has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The vote was strictly partisan.
Washington has gotten more partisan every year.
He wrote a history of partisan warfare in Yugoslavia.
Partisan units operated out of the forests.

senses.head: Strongly supporting one political party, often blindly
examples: The vote was strictly partisan.
Washington has gotten more partisan every year.

senses.head: Of irregular fighters resisting an occupying army
examples: He wrote a history of partisan warfare in Yugoslavia.
Partisan units operated out of the forests.

entries.contrast: A false friend. In American political news a partisan is a party loyalist, not a партизан; the fighter sense survives mostly in history writing. Also a noun.

entries.meaning: Passable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He speaks passable Spanish.
The food was passable and the view was great.
The road is passable again now that the plows came through.
Only one bridge was still passable.

senses.head: Good enough, but no better than that
examples: He speaks passable Spanish.
The food was passable and the view was great.

senses.head: That you can travel on or through
examples: The road is passable again now that the plows came through.
Only one bridge was still passable.

entries.meaning: No longer fashionable. ---
examples: Fondue parties were passe by 1980.
He thinks neckties are passe.
Nothing looks more passe than last year's slang.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: that look is passe
entries.form: from French; usually printed with the accent, passé
entries.contrast: A little bookish, and always about fashions and tastes, not about machines: say an outdated printer, not a passe printer.

entries.meaning: Passing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He made a passing remark about moving.
She had a passing interest in chess and then dropped it.
A 70 is a passing grade.
He needs a passing score to graduate.

senses.head: Lasting only a moment, or done quickly and without much attention
examples: He made a passing remark about moving.
She had a passing interest in chess and then dropped it.

senses.head: Good enough to pass a test or a class
examples: A 70 is a passing grade.
He needs a passing score to graduate.

entries.position: attributive only — a passing remark, a passing grade

entries.meaning: Passionate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They had a passionate argument about the budget.
She gave a passionate speech to the council.
He's passionate about teaching.
I've never met anyone more passionate about birds.

senses.head: Feeling or showing very strong emotion
examples: They had a passionate argument about the budget.
She gave a passionate speech to the council.

senses.head: Caring very much about something you do
examples: He's passionate about teaching.
I've never met anyone more passionate about birds.

entries.meaning: Passive has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He stayed passive while the others argued about the bill.
Her passive attitude toward the problem frustrated everyone.
Kids get more passive the longer they sit in front of a screen.
The sentence The window was broken uses the passive voice.
Teachers often tell students to avoid the passive voice.
In a passive construction the doer may not be mentioned at all.
Passive income lets him work three days a week.
Passive smoking is dangerous for small children.

senses.head: Accepting what happens without acting or resisting
examples: He stayed passive while the others argued about the bill.
Her passive attitude toward the problem frustrated everyone.
Kids get more passive the longer they sit in front of a screen.

senses.head: In grammar, of a verb form in which the subject receives the action
examples: The sentence The window was broken uses the passive voice.
Teachers often tell students to avoid the passive voice.
In a passive construction the doer may not be mentioned at all.

senses.head: Working with no active effort, power or equipment
examples: Passive income lets him work three days a week.
Passive smoking is dangerous for small children.

entries.meaning: No longer fashionable. ---
examples: Those jeans are passé.
He said email was passé, which surprised the room.
Calling it a blog feels a little passé now.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always after a verb: That style is passé
entries.form: from French; American writing usually keeps the accent: passé

entries.meaning: Past has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I've been sick for the past few days.
Over the past year the company has doubled in size.
Past experience tells me not to trust that website.
She is a past president of the association.
The award goes to a past winner every tenth year.

senses.head: Gone by; belonging to the time before now
examples: I've been sick for the past few days.
Over the past year the company has doubled in size.
Past experience tells me not to trust that website.

senses.head: Former — holding a position earlier but not now
examples: She is a past president of the association.
The award goes to a past winner every tenth year.

entries.position: both — nearly always before a noun; Those days are past is formal
entries.contrast: Past is also a preposition (drive past the school) and a noun (in the past); only the use with a noun is the adjective.

entries.meaning: Soft and pale in color. ---
examples: The nursery is painted in pastel colors.
She wore a pastel blue dress to the wedding.
The walls are pastel, which makes the room feel bigger.
entries.contrast: Pastel is also a noun — a soft chalk for drawing, and the drawing made with it.

entries.meaning: Heated to kill harmful bacteria, so that it keeps longer. ---
examples: Only pasteurized milk is sold in American supermarkets.
The cheese is made from milk that has not been pasteurized.
Check the label to see whether the juice is pasteurized.

entries.meaning: Pastoral has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The painting shows a pastoral scene with sheep and a stream.
He writes pastoral poetry about the farm where he grew up.
The church offers pastoral counseling to families.
Pastoral duties take up most of her week.

senses.head: Showing country life as pleasant and peaceful
examples: The painting shows a pastoral scene with sheep and a stream.
He writes pastoral poetry about the farm where he grew up.

senses.head: Relating to a priest's or minister's care for people
examples: The church offers pastoral counseling to families.
Pastoral duties take up most of her week.

entries.meaning: Pasty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He looked pasty after a week indoors.
By February everyone's face is pastier than it was in July.
She has a pasty complexion that burns in ten minutes.
The sauce turned pasty as it cooled.
Add water until the powder is no longer pasty.

senses.head: Pale and unhealthy-looking
examples: He looked pasty after a week indoors.
By February everyone's face is pastier than it was in July.
She has a pasty complexion that burns in ten minutes.

senses.head: Thick and sticky, like paste
examples: The sauce turned pasty as it cooled.
Add water until the powder is no longer pasty.

entries.contrast: The British noun pasty (a meat pie) rhymes with nasty; the adjective rhymes with tasty.

entries.meaning: Too quick and easy to be convincing; sounding prepared in advance. ---
examples: He gave a pat answer that satisfied nobody.
The movie ends with a pat solution to a serious problem.
Her explanation sounded a little too pat.
entries.contrast: Don't confuse the adjective with the verb pat (pat the dog) or the idiom have it down pat, meaning 'know it perfectly'.

entries.meaning: Patchy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Patchy fog is expected along the coast tonight.
The grass is patchy where the dog sleeps.
His knowledge of the subject is patchy.
Cell service gets patchier the farther you drive.

senses.head: Appearing in separate small areas rather than evenly
examples: Patchy fog is expected along the coast tonight.
The grass is patchy where the dog sleeps.

senses.head: Good in some parts and bad in others
examples: His knowledge of the subject is patchy.
Cell service gets patchier the farther you drive.

entries.meaning: Patent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: That is patent nonsense and everyone in the room knew it.
The article contained a patent lie about the mayor.
She wore black patent shoes with the dress.
The purse is made of red patent leather.

senses.head: Completely obvious; impossible to deny
examples: That is patent nonsense and everyone in the room knew it.
The article contained a patent lie about the mayor.

senses.head: Of leather: treated to have a hard, shiny surface
examples: She wore black patent shoes with the dress.
The purse is made of red patent leather.

entries.contrast: Patent is far more common as a noun and a verb (file a patent, patent an invention).

entries.meaning: Patented has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The company uses a patented process to purify the water.
Their patented design keeps the cup from tipping over.
He greeted us with his patented grin.
She answered with her patented mix of charm and steel.

senses.head: Protected by a patent, so that only the owner may make or sell it
examples: The company uses a patented process to purify the water.
Their patented design keeps the cup from tipping over.

senses.head: Informal: unmistakably a particular person's own
examples: He greeted us with his patented grin.
She answered with her patented mix of charm and steel.

entries.meaning: Paternal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He felt a surge of paternal pride at the graduation.
The coach takes a paternal interest in his players.
My paternal grandmother came from Poland.
The condition is passed down through the paternal line.

senses.head: Like a father; showing a father's care
examples: He felt a surge of paternal pride at the graduation.
The coach takes a paternal interest in his players.

senses.head: Related through the father
examples: My paternal grandmother came from Poland.
The condition is passed down through the paternal line.

entries.meaning: Making decisions for other people as if they could not decide for themselves. ---
examples: The policy is well meant but deeply paternalistic.
Patients resent a paternalistic doctor who won't explain anything.
Older companies tend to be more paternalistic toward their workers.

entries.meaning: Pathological has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He is a pathological liar — he can't help it.
She has a pathological fear of being late.
The lab found no pathological changes in the tissue.
Pathological tests confirmed the diagnosis.

senses.head: Unable to stop doing something, in a way that seems like an illness
examples: He is a pathological liar — he can't help it.
She has a pathological fear of being late.

senses.head: Relating to disease and its causes
examples: The lab found no pathological changes in the tissue.
Pathological tests confirmed the diagnosis.

entries.meaning: Controlled by men, or organized so that men hold the power. ---
examples: She grew up in a strongly patriarchal household.
The novel is a quiet attack on a patriarchal society.
Village life there is still more patriarchal than in the capital.

entries.meaning: Belonging to or typical of the upper class. ---
examples: He speaks with a patrician accent.
Her patrician manners set her apart at the meeting.
The family lived in a patrician house above the river.
entries.contrast: Patrician is also a noun — a member of the old Roman nobility.

entries.meaning: Feeling or showing strong love for one's country. ---
examples: The Fourth of July is full of patriotic songs and parades.
He isn't patriotic about much, but he loves the anthem.
Nothing makes her feel more patriotic than the Olympics.

entries.meaning: Treating someone as if they were less intelligent or important than you. ---
examples: Don't use that patronizing tone with me.
The article is patronizing toward first-time voters.
Explaining it a third time would be patronizing.
entries.contrast: The verb patronize has a second, neutral meaning — to be a regular customer of a store.

entries.meaning: Patterned has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She chose a patterned wallpaper for the hallway.
The chairs are patterned, so the rug should be plain.
The new law is patterned after the one in California.
Their school is patterned on a British boarding school.

senses.head: Decorated with a repeated design
examples: She chose a patterned wallpaper for the hallway.
The chairs are patterned, so the rug should be plain.

senses.head: Made to follow the model of something else
examples: The new law is patterned after the one in California.
Their school is patterned on a British boarding school.

entries.русский: узорчатый, с рисунком; созданный по образцу
entries.takes: after or on + noun, in the 'copied from' sense

entries.meaning: Covered with a hard surface such as asphalt, concrete or stone. ---
examples: Turn left where the road becomes paved.
A paved path leads down to the lake.
Their driveway is paved with red brick.

entries.meaning: Happening automatically, as a trained reaction to a signal. ---
examples: My dog has a Pavlovian response to the sound of the can opener.
Checking the phone the second it buzzes is a Pavlovian reflex.
The ad works on a simple Pavlovian association.

entries.meaning: That must be paid, or may be paid, at a stated time or to a stated person. ---
examples: The deposit is payable when you sign the lease.
Make the check payable to the county clerk.
There is a small fee payable on delivery.

He put together a polyglot edition of the poem.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a polyglot city
entries.contrast: Polyglot is also a noun for a person who speaks many languages: She's a polyglot — five languages.

entries.meaning: From the islands of Polynesia in the central Pacific. ---
examples: The museum has a room of Polynesian carvings.
Polynesian navigators crossed the Pacific in canoes.
Much of the island's music is Polynesian in origin.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a person: She's Polynesian on her mother's side.

entries.meaning: Believing in many gods. ---
examples: Ancient Greek religion was polytheistic.
The empire tolerated polytheistic worship for centuries.
Hinduism looks polytheistic from the outside, though many Hindus disagree.

entries.meaning: Of a fat or oil: of the kind considered better for the heart. ---
examples: Sunflower oil is high in polyunsaturated fat.
The label lists polyunsaturated and saturated fats separately.
Doctors recommend polyunsaturated oils instead of butter.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: polyunsaturated fats

entries.meaning: Acting more important than you are, especially in the way you talk. ---
examples: The speech was long and pompous.
He is a pompous man who asks to be called Doctor at dinner.
Nobody at the table was more pompous than the host.

entries.meaning: Ponderous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The elephant turned with ponderous dignity.
A ponderous truck blocked the whole street.
The book is ponderous and could lose a hundred pages.
His lectures are more ponderous than his articles.

senses.head: Heavy and slow-moving
examples: The elephant turned with ponderous dignity.
A ponderous truck blocked the whole street.

senses.head: Dull and far too serious — of writing or speech
examples: The book is ponderous and could lose a hundred pages.
His lectures are more ponderous than his articles.

entries.meaning: Popular has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is the most popular teacher in the school.
The app is especially popular with college students.
He won the popular vote but lost the election.
Popular opinion has shifted on the issue.

senses.head: Liked by a lot of people
examples: She is the most popular teacher in the school.
The app is especially popular with college students.

senses.head: Of or for ordinary people; general
examples: He won the popular vote but lost the election.
Popular opinion has shifted on the issue.

entries.contrast: Popular means liked by many people; populous means having many people living there: the most populous state, not the most popular state.

entries.meaning: Lived in by people — normally with a word saying how many. ---
examples: The coast is densely populated.
They moved to a sparsely populated part of Montana.
The eastern half of the state is far more populated than the west.
entries.position: both — almost always with an adverb: densely populated, sparsely populated

entries.meaning: Having a large number of people living there. ---
examples: California is the most populous state in the country.
China was the world's most populous nation for centuries.
The delta is populous and very hard to evacuate.
entries.contrast: Not popular. Populous = with many people living there; popular = liked by many people.

entries.meaning: Showing sexual acts in a way meant to excite people. ---
examples: The site was shut down for hosting pornographic material.
The court had to decide whether the film was pornographic.
He was fired for keeping pornographic images on a work computer.
entries.form: -ic from pornography; shortened to porn in speech

entries.meaning: Porous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Sandstone is porous, so it soaks up water.
Use a sealer on the porous side of the tile.
The border is long and porous.
Their defense got more porous in the second half.

senses.head: Full of tiny holes that let liquid or air through
examples: Sandstone is porous, so it soaks up water.
Use a sealer on the porous side of the tile.

senses.head: Easy to get through or across — of a border or a defense
examples: The border is long and porous.
Their defense got more porous in the second half.

entries.meaning: Portable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She travels with a portable speaker.
The newer machine is smaller and far more portable.
His pension is portable if he changes employers.
Coding is a portable skill.

senses.head: Light and easy to carry around
examples: She travels with a portable speaker.
The newer machine is smaller and far more portable.

senses.head: Able to be taken from one job or country to another — of benefits or skills
examples: His pension is portable if he changes employers.
Coding is a portable skill.

entries.contrast: In American schools a portable is also a noun — a temporary classroom trailer.

entries.meaning: Rather fat — usually said of a middle-aged man. ---
examples: A portly gentleman in a vest showed us to our seats.
He has grown portly since he stopped playing ball.
The older brother is the portlier of the two.
entries.contrast: A polite, slightly old-fashioned word for a heavy man; it is not used about women. Like friendly and lonely, it ends in -ly but is an adjective.

entries.meaning: From Portugal, or in the language of Portugal and Brazil. ---
examples: They ordered a bottle of Portuguese wine.
Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country.
The tiles on the church are clearly Portuguese.
entries.contrast: Also a noun — the language (She speaks Portuguese) and the people (the Portuguese). The plural has no -s: one Portuguese, two Portuguese.

entries.meaning: Expensive and elegant. ---
examples: They had dinner at a posh restaurant on the waterfront.
Her new place is a lot posher than the old one.
It's a posh neighborhood with gates at both ends.
entries.contrast: The word came from British English. Americans use it about expensive places and things (a posh hotel), not about a person's accent the way the British do.

entries.meaning: Positive has 4 distinct senses.
examples: The reviews have been more positive than we expected.
Try to stay positive about the move.
I'm positive I locked the door.
Are you positive it was him?
Her test came back positive.
Two players tested positive the day before the game.
Multiply the two positive numbers first.
Connect the red wire to the positive terminal.

senses.head: Good, hopeful, or helpful
examples: The reviews have been more positive than we expected.
Try to stay positive about the move.

senses.head: Completely sure
examples: I'm positive I locked the door.
Are you positive it was him?

senses.head: Showing that a substance or an illness is there — of a test
examples: Her test came back positive.
Two players tested positive the day before the game.

senses.head: Greater than zero, or carrying the charge of a proton
examples: Multiply the two positive numbers first.
Connect the red wire to the positive terminal.

entries.takes: about + noun or -ing; that-clause (in the sure sense)

entries.meaning: Possessed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The villagers believed the girl was possessed.
He worked like a man possessed for three days straight.
She is possessed of a sharp memory and a sharper tongue.
The family was possessed of a large fortune.

senses.head: Controlled by an evil spirit, or acting as if you were
examples: The villagers believed the girl was possessed.
He worked like a man possessed for three days straight.

senses.head: Formal: having a quality or a thing
examples: She is possessed of a sharp memory and a sharper tongue.
The family was possessed of a large fortune.

entries.position: predicative only — after a verb, or straight after the noun: he fought like a man possessed
entries.takes: by + a spirit; formal of + noun (= having)
entries.contrast: Possessed of is a formal way of saying having: She is possessed of enormous patience. Do not confuse it with possessive.

entries.meaning: Possessive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her boyfriend is so possessive that he texts her all day.
The dog gets possessive about his bowl.
He was always possessive of his little sister.
Possessive pronouns include my, your and their.
Add an apostrophe to make the noun possessive.

senses.head: Wanting to keep someone or something entirely for yourself
examples: Her boyfriend is so possessive that he texts her all day.
The dog gets possessive about his bowl.
He was always possessive of his little sister.

senses.head: In grammar, showing that something belongs to someone
examples: Possessive pronouns include my, your and their.
Add an apostrophe to make the noun possessive.

entries.meaning: Relating to the mail and the service that carries it. ---
examples: Postal rates went up again in January.
Postal workers are out delivering even in the snow.
The postal service delivers to every address in the country.
entries.contrast: Go postal is slang for losing your temper violently — it comes from shootings at US post offices in the 1980s and 90s, and it is the one place the word follows a verb.

entries.meaning: Done after finishing a doctorate. ---
examples: She has a postdoctoral fellowship at MIT.
He spent two years doing postdoctoral research in chemistry.
Postdoctoral positions in the sciences are hard to get.
entries.contrast: Everyone shortens it to postdoc, which is both an adjective (a postdoc position) and a noun for the researcher.

entries.meaning: Done after a first university degree. ---
examples: He went on to postgraduate study in London.
She has a postgraduate degree in economics.
The hospital runs a postgraduate training program for surgeons.
entries.contrast: In the US the everyday word is graduate: graduate school, a graduate degree. Postgraduate is mainly British, though American medicine keeps postgraduate training for doctors who already have a degree.

entries.meaning: Happening or published after someone has died. ---
examples: He received a posthumous Medal of Honor.
The album was a posthumous release.
Her posthumous novel became a bestseller.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable and the h is silent: PAHS-chuh-muhs, never pohst-HYOO-muhs.

entries.meaning: Belonging to a time or place where heavy industry has closed down and services matter more. ---
examples: Detroit is often called a postindustrial city.
We live in a postindustrial economy built on services.
The whole valley is postindustrial now — the mills are apartments.

entries.meaning: Past menopause; relating to the years after it. ---
examples: The study followed four hundred postmenopausal women.
Postmenopausal women lose bone density faster.
Once a woman is postmenopausal, her risk of heart disease rises.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the style in art, writing and building that plays with older styles and doubts big explanations. ---
examples: The building is a famous piece of postmodern architecture.
Her novels are playful and postmodern.
He teaches a class on postmodern literature.

entries.meaning: Happening in the period after an operation. ---
examples: She stayed in postoperative care for two days.
Postoperative pain is normal for the first week.
The nurse went over the postoperative instructions.
entries.contrast: In hospital speech it is shortened to post-op: the post-op ward.

entries.meaning: Happening in the weeks after a woman gives birth. ---
examples: She was treated for postpartum depression.
The postpartum checkup is six weeks after the birth.
Many new mothers get postpartum anxiety and don't talk about it.
entries.form: from Latin post partum, 'after the birth'

entries.meaning: Belonging to the years after a war, usually the Second World War. ---
examples: The postwar years brought a huge building boom.
Postwar Germany was divided in two.
He grew up in postwar Japan.

entries.meaning: Clean enough to drink safely. ---
examples: The sign said the water was not potable.
Campers should carry potable water.
Only half the village has potable water.
entries.contrast: A formal word on signs and in reports; in speech Americans say drinking water or safe to drink. It has nothing to do with portable.

entries.meaning: Having a round belly that sticks out. ---
examples: A potbellied man in an undershirt answered the door.
They keep a potbellied pig as a pet.
The potbellied stove kept the whole cabin warm.

entries.meaning: Potent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: This is a very potent painkiller — one pill is enough.
The cleaner is potent, so open a window.
Fear is a potent political weapon.
The flag is still a potent symbol for them.

senses.head: Strong in its effect, especially a drug, a drink or a chemical
examples: This is a very potent painkiller — one pill is enough.
The cleaner is potent, so open a window.

senses.head: Powerful in its influence on people or events
examples: Fear is a potent political weapon.
The flag is still a potent symbol for them.

entries.meaning: Possible, though not real or certain yet. ---
examples: We've found three potential buyers for the house.
Every potential risk has to be listed in the report.
She's a potential candidate for the job.
entries.contrast: Only before a noun: say a potential problem, never The problem is potential. The noun potential is different — it means the ability to develop: She has great potential.

entries.meaning: Growing in a flowerpot rather than in the ground. ---
examples: She keeps a potted fern by the window.
The porch is full of potted plants.
He gave her a potted orchid for her birthday.
entries.form: -ed from pot, with the t doubled
entries.contrast: British English also uses potted for food kept in a pot (potted shrimp) and for a short version of something (a potted history); Americans use neither.

entries.meaning: Taught to use the toilet, said of a small child. ---
examples: Is your daughter potty-trained yet?
He wasn't fully potty-trained until he was three.
The preschool only takes potty-trained kids.
entries.form: compound — noun + past participle: potty + trained

entries.meaning: Extremely poor. ---
examples: She grew up in a poverty-stricken neighborhood.
The region was poverty-stricken long before the war.
Aid workers describe whole villages as poverty-stricken.
entries.form: compound — noun + past participle: poverty + stricken, an old participle of strike

entries.meaning: Powdered has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The recipe calls for powdered sugar.
We mixed powdered milk with warm water.
He came back with a box of powdered doughnuts.
The judges in the painting wear powdered wigs.

senses.head: Made into or sold as a dry powder
examples: The recipe calls for powdered sugar.
We mixed powdered milk with warm water.

senses.head: Covered with a fine powder
examples: He came back with a box of powdered doughnuts.
The judges in the painting wear powdered wigs.

entries.meaning: Like powder — dry, fine and loose. ---
examples: The snow was light and powdery.
There was a powdery white residue in the sink.
The old chocolate had a powdery gray coating.

entries.meaning: Driven by a motor or by the source of energy named in the compound. ---
examples: The toy is battery-powered.
He gets around in a powered wheelchair.
The whole house is solar-powered.
entries.position: both — very often the second half of a compound: battery-powered, solar-powered

entries.meaning: Powerful has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She's one of the most powerful people in Washington.
The industry has a powerful lobby behind it.
The truck has a powerful engine.
He has powerful shoulders from years of swimming.
It's a powerful film about losing a parent.
Her speech was simple but powerful.

senses.head: Having a lot of control or influence over people and events
examples: She's one of the most powerful people in Washington.
The industry has a powerful lobby behind it.

senses.head: Physically strong, or strong in effect
examples: The truck has a powerful engine.
He has powerful shoulders from years of swimming.

senses.head: Having a strong effect on your feelings
examples: It's a powerful film about losing a parent.
Her speech was simple but powerful.

entries.meaning: Unable to control or stop what is happening. ---
examples: The police were powerless to stop the crowd.
Small farmers feel powerless against the big buyers.
Watching and not helping is a powerless feeling.

entries.meaning: Able to be done in the real world. ---
examples: We'll move the meeting as soon as it is practicable.
The engineers said the design was not practicable.
Repairs must be made at the earliest practicable date.
entries.contrast: Not the same as practical. Practicable means it can be done at all; practical means it is sensible and worth doing. A plan can be practicable but not practical. The word is formal and mostly written.

entries.meaning: Practical has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She's more practical than her brother — she reads the manual first.
Be practical: you can't carry all that on a bike.
Is there a practical way to fix this without spending money?
Those shoes are pretty but not very practical.
The course gives students practical experience in a real clinic.
In practical terms, nothing will change.

senses.head: Sensible and good at dealing with real situations
examples: She's more practical than her brother — she reads the manual first.
Be practical: you can't carry all that on a bike.

senses.head: Useful and likely to work
examples: Is there a practical way to fix this without spending money?
Those shoes are pretty but not very practical.

senses.head: Involving real doing rather than ideas or theory
examples: The course gives students practical experience in a real clinic.
In practical terms, nothing will change.

entries.contrast: Keep it apart from practicable, which only means 'possible to do'.

entries.meaning: Done so often that it looks easy and automatic. ---
examples: He opened the lock with a practiced hand.
She gave a practiced smile to the camera.
He's practiced at talking his way out of trouble.
entries.contrast: American English spells both the noun and the verb practice, so the adjective is always practiced; the British write practised.

entries.meaning: Dealing with things in a practical, realistic way rather than by theory or principle. ---
examples: She took a pragmatic approach and fixed the cheapest problems first.
We have to be pragmatic about what we can afford.
His decision was pragmatic rather than moral.
entries.contrast: In Russian прагматичный can sound selfish; in English pragmatic is nearly always a compliment — it means realistic about what will actually work.

entries.meaning: Deserving praise. ---
examples: Her effort to learn the language was praiseworthy.
The report mentions several praiseworthy programs.
Volunteering on weekends is praiseworthy, but it won't fix the problem.

entries.meaning: Already there before the time being talked about. ---
examples: Insurers can't turn you down for a pre-existing condition.
The crack was a pre-existing problem, not our fault.
The new law builds on pre-existing rules.
entries.contrast: Written both ways. Pre-existing with the hyphen is the usual spelling in American health-insurance and legal writing; preexisting is the same word.

entries.meaning: Telling other people how they should behave, in a way that annoys them. ---
examples: The film is good until it turns preachy at the end.
I don't want to sound preachy, but you should really call her.
The second half of the book gets preachier and preachier.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — preachier, preachiest; also more preachy, most preachy

entries.meaning: Likely to turn into cancer if it is left alone. ---
examples: The doctor removed a precancerous mole.
The cells were precancerous but not yet cancer.
Screening catches precancerous changes early.

entries.meaning: Precarious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The ladder was in a precarious position against the wall.
The vase looked precarious on the edge of the table.
Thousands of families are in a precarious financial situation.
His hold on power is precarious.

senses.head: Not held firmly and likely to fall
examples: The ladder was in a precarious position against the wall.
The vase looked precarious on the edge of the table.

senses.head: Uncertain and likely to get worse at any moment
examples: Thousands of families are in a precarious financial situation.
His hold on power is precarious.

entries.meaning: Done to stop something bad from happening, even if it probably won't. ---
examples: The school closed as a precautionary measure.
They gave him antibiotics as a precautionary step.
The evacuation was purely precautionary.

entries.meaning: Coming just before the one being talked about. ---
examples: See the table on the preceding page.
Sales fell in the three preceding months.
The preceding chapter explains the method.
entries.contrast: Preceding comes before, following comes after. In speech Americans usually say previous or the one before.

entries.meaning: Precious has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Gold and silver are precious metals.
She keeps her precious stones in a safe.
Every hour of daylight was precious.
Those photos are precious to me.
The dialogue is a little precious for my taste.
He has a precious way of talking about his art.

senses.head: Rare and worth a lot of money
examples: Gold and silver are precious metals.
She keeps her precious stones in a safe.

senses.head: Loved or valued so much that you don't want to lose it
examples: Every hour of daylight was precious.
Those photos are precious to me.

senses.head: Too refined and delicate, in a way that annoys people
examples: The dialogue is a little precious for my taste.
He has a precious way of talking about his art.

entries.meaning: Precipitous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The trail runs along a precipitous cliff.
The road down the mountain was narrow and precipitous.
Sales took a precipitous drop in March.
The company's precipitous decline surprised everyone.

senses.head: Very steep, so that you could fall a long way
examples: The trail runs along a precipitous cliff.
The road down the mountain was narrow and precipitous.

senses.head: Sudden and very large, said of a fall or a decline
examples: Sales took a precipitous drop in March.
The company's precipitous decline surprised everyone.

entries.contrast: Don't mix it with the adjective precipitate, which means done too suddenly and without thinking: a precipitate decision.

entries.meaning: Precise has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Can you be more precise about the time?
The instructions are very precise.
At that precise moment the phone rang.
Those were his precise words.

senses.head: Exact and clearly stated, with nothing left vague
examples: Can you be more precise about the time?
The instructions are very precise.

senses.head: Before a noun, emphasizing that it is exactly that one
examples: At that precise moment the phone rang.
Those were his precise words.

entries.contrast: Precise is not the same as accurate: a measurement can be precise (very finely stated) and still be wrong. To be precise is a set phrase used to correct yourself.

entries.meaning: More developed or more grown-up than is usual at that age. ---
examples: She was a precocious reader — novels at six.
His son is precocious and a little exhausting.
The movie is full of precocious kids saying adult things.
entries.contrast: Almost always about a child. It can carry a hint of criticism, as if the child were showing off.

entries.meaning: Formed in your head before you knew anything about the case. ---
examples: Try to come in without preconceived ideas.
She had preconceived notions about small towns.
Our preconceived opinions got in the way.
entries.contrast: It goes almost only with idea, notion or opinion.

entries.meaning: Predatory has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Hawks and owls are predatory birds.
Predatory fish keep the lake in balance.
The law was written to stop predatory lending.
His behavior toward younger employees was predatory.

senses.head: Living by hunting and eating other animals
examples: Hawks and owls are predatory birds.
Predatory fish keep the lake in balance.

senses.head: Taking advantage of weaker people for money or power
examples: The law was written to stop predatory lending.
His behavior toward younger employees was predatory.

entries.meaning: Decided in advance by fate or by God, so that it cannot be changed. ---
examples: He felt predestined to be a teacher.
They believed the whole thing was predestined.
She was predestined for a life on the stage.

entries.meaning: Decided or fixed before it happens. ---
examples: The route was predetermined before we left.
Payments are made on predetermined dates.
The outcome felt predetermined from the start.

entries.meaning: Predictable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Traffic here is predictable — always bad at five.
The result was entirely predictable.
The ending of the movie was sadly predictable.
He's so predictable: same order, same table, every week.

senses.head: Able to be known in advance because it always goes the same way
examples: Traffic here is predictable — always bad at five.
The result was entirely predictable.

senses.head: Boring because it never surprises anyone
examples: The ending of the movie was sadly predictable.
He's so predictable: same order, same table, every week.

entries.meaning: Used to work out in advance what will happen. ---
examples: The company uses predictive analytics to plan its stock.
Turn off predictive text if it keeps guessing wrong.
Test scores are not predictive of success at work.

entries.meaning: Likely to get an illness, or to think or act a certain way, before anything happens. ---
examples: Some people are genetically predisposed to diabetes.
He was predisposed to like her before they even met.
Voters were already predisposed toward change.
entries.takes: to + noun or -ing; to-infinitive; toward + noun

entries.meaning: Larger in number or stronger in influence than all the others. ---
examples: Spanish is the predominant language in the neighborhood.
Blue is the predominant color in the painting.
In the older group, joint pain was predominant.
entries.contrast: The adverb predominantly is far more common than the adjective: The crowd was predominantly young.

entries.meaning: Better known and more respected than anyone else in the field. ---
examples: She is the preeminent heart surgeon in the country.
The museum holds a preeminent collection of Dutch painting.
For decades he was the preeminent voice on the subject.
entries.contrast: Also written pre-eminent; the spelling without the hyphen is now standard in American writing.

entries.meaning: Done first, to stop someone else from acting. ---
examples: The army launched a preemptive strike.
She sent a preemptive email before anyone could complain.
It was a preemptive move to protect the company.
entries.contrast: Also written pre-emptive. The adverb preemptively is just as common: She apologized preemptively.

entries.meaning: Already in place before the event or agreement being discussed. ---
examples: The building had preexisting damage from the last storm.
Their deal replaced a preexisting contract.
Preexisting cracks in the wall got worse over the winter.
entries.contrast: The hyphenated pre-existing is the more common American spelling, especially in writing about health insurance; both are correct.

entries.meaning: Built from parts made in a factory and put together on the site. ---
examples: They put up a prefab garage in a weekend.
The cabins are prefab and cost half as much.
He lives in a prefab house from the 1950s.
entries.contrast: Prefab is also a noun for the building itself: a row of prefabs.

entries.meaning: Better, or more suitable, than the other choice. ---
examples: Walking is preferable to sitting in traffic.
A short delay is preferable to a bad decision.
It would be preferable to meet in person.
entries.comparison: not gradable — the word already means 'better', so never more preferable
entries.form: -able from prefer, with the stress moving back to the first syllable
entries.contrast: Two traps: never more preferable, and never preferable than — it is always preferable to. The stress is PREF-ur-uh-buhl, not pri-FUR-uh-buhl.

entries.meaning: Giving one person or group better treatment than the rest. ---
examples: Members get preferential treatment at the door.
The deal gave the company preferential access to the market.
He denied giving his friends preferential rates.

entries.meaning: Liked or chosen more than the others. ---
examples: What's your preferred method of payment?
Email is her preferred way to be reached.
The form asks for your preferred name.
entries.form: -ed from prefer; the r doubles because the stress is on the last syllable

entries.meaning: Prehistoric has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cave has prehistoric paintings on the walls.
Prehistoric people hunted these animals.
His phone is practically prehistoric.
The computers in that office are prehistoric.

senses.head: From the time before events were written down
examples: The cave has prehistoric paintings on the walls.
Prehistoric people hunted these animals.

senses.head: Joking: hopelessly old-fashioned
examples: His phone is practically prehistoric.
The computers in that office are prehistoric.

entries.meaning: Holding an unfair opinion about a group of people without good reason. ---
examples: He's prejudiced against anyone under thirty.
The judge was accused of being prejudiced.
It's hard to win over a prejudiced jury.
entries.takes: against + noun; in favor of + noun
entries.contrast: A person is prejudiced; a piece of evidence or a news story is prejudicial. The two are not interchangeable.

entries.meaning: Likely to damage someone's case or turn people against them unfairly. ---
examples: The defense argued that the photos were prejudicial.
Releasing the tape would be prejudicial to a fair trial.
The judge excluded the prejudicial evidence.
entries.contrast: Mostly a legal word, and not a synonym of prejudiced: people are prejudiced, evidence is prejudicial.

entries.meaning: Coming first, before the main or final part. ---
examples: The preliminary results look good.
There will be a preliminary hearing on Monday.
These figures are preliminary and may change.

entries.meaning: Happening before a marriage. ---
examples: They signed a premarital agreement.
The church offers premarital counseling.
The survey asked about premarital sex.

entries.meaning: Premature has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's premature to celebrate — the votes aren't counted.
His premature announcement caused a lot of confusion.
The baby was six weeks premature.
Premature babies stay in the hospital longer.

senses.head: Happening too soon, before the right time
examples: It's premature to celebrate — the votes aren't counted.
His premature announcement caused a lot of confusion.

senses.head: Born before the expected date
examples: The baby was six weeks premature.
Premature babies stay in the hospital longer.

entries.meaning: Planned in advance rather than done on the spur of the moment. ---
examples: He was charged with premeditated murder.
The attack was premeditated, not a sudden fight.
Her apology sounded premeditated.

entries.meaning: Happening in the days before a woman's period. ---
examples: She gets premenstrual headaches.
Premenstrual symptoms usually stop once the period starts.
The doctor asked about premenstrual mood changes.
entries.contrast: PMS stands for premenstrual syndrome and is what people actually say.

entries.meaning: Best or most important of its kind. ---
examples: It's the premier jazz club in the city.
She trained at the country's premier dance school.
The prize goes to the premier researcher in the field.
entries.contrast: The noun premier (a head of government) sounds the same. Premiere, with the final -e, is the first showing of a movie or play — a different word.

entries.meaning: Of higher quality and costing more than the standard kind. ---
examples: The car takes premium gas.
They sell a premium version with more features.
You pay extra for premium seats.
entries.contrast: As a noun, a premium is what you pay for insurance, or an extra amount: Buyers paid a premium for the view.

entries.meaning: Happening before a baby is born, while the mother is pregnant. ---
examples: She takes prenatal vitamins every morning.
Good prenatal care lowers the risk to the baby.
The clinic offers free prenatal classes.
entries.contrast: American English says prenatal; British English says antenatal.

entries.meaning: Made or done before a wedding, usually about money and property. ---
examples: They signed a prenuptial agreement before the wedding.
His lawyer drew up a prenuptial contract.
Prenuptial agreements are common among business owners.
entries.contrast: Americans shorten prenuptial agreement to a prenup, which is a noun: They signed a prenup.

entries.meaning: Thinking so hard about one thing that you don't notice anything else. ---
examples: He seemed preoccupied all through dinner.
She's preoccupied with money right now.
You've got that preoccupied look again.
entries.contrast: Preoccupied is about a mind that is full of one worry, not about having a lot to do — for that say busy or tied up.

entries.meaning: Prepackaged has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The store sells prepackaged salads.
Everything in the vending machine is prepackaged.
The candidate gave prepackaged answers to every question.
The whole apology felt prepackaged.

senses.head: Put in its package at the factory, before it reaches the store
examples: The store sells prepackaged salads.
Everything in the vending machine is prepackaged.

senses.head: Prepared in advance and not genuine or original
examples: The candidate gave prepackaged answers to every question.
The whole apology felt prepackaged.

entries.meaning: Paid for before it is used or sent. ---
examples: She bought a prepaid phone card.
Send it back in the prepaid envelope.
The shipping is prepaid, so it costs you nothing.
entries.form: pre- + paid, the past participle of pay

entries.meaning: Done in order to get ready for something else. ---
examples: He did a year of preparatory work before applying.
Preparatory schools get students ready for college.
The preparatory meetings took months.
entries.contrast: Preparatory school is almost always shortened to prep school.

entries.meaning: Prepared has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Are you prepared for the test?
We weren't prepared for how cold it would be.
I'm not prepared to pay that much.
She said she was prepared to resign.
He read a prepared statement to the press.
The lecture used prepared slides.

senses.head: Ready, because you have got everything done in advance
examples: Are you prepared for the test?
We weren't prepared for how cold it would be.

senses.head: Willing to do something
examples: I'm not prepared to pay that much.
She said she was prepared to resign.

senses.head: Made or written in advance
examples: He read a prepared statement to the press.
The lecture used prepared slides.

entries.meaning: So silly that it does not deserve to be taken seriously. ---
examples: The whole idea is preposterous.
He made a preposterous claim about the moon landing.
It's preposterous to blame the weather for this.

entries.meaning: Recorded in advance instead of being broadcast or played live. ---
examples: The interview was prerecorded.
A prerecorded message told us to hold.
They played a prerecorded segment during the show.

entries.meaning: Showing that someone knew in advance how things would turn out. ---
examples: Her warning about the housing market turned out to be prescient.
He was prescient about how the internet would change the news.
The novel now looks strangely prescient.
entries.contrast: A formal, mostly written word; in speech Americans say He saw it coming.

entries.meaning: Prescribed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Take the prescribed dose twice a day.
She stopped her prescribed medication without telling anyone.
Fill out the form in the prescribed manner.
The fee is prescribed by law.

senses.head: Ordered by a doctor as treatment
examples: Take the prescribed dose twice a day.
She stopped her prescribed medication without telling anyone.

senses.head: Laid down officially as the rule to follow
examples: Fill out the form in the prescribed manner.
The fee is prescribed by law.

entries.contrast: Prescribe means a doctor orders something; proscribe means to forbid it. So prescribed and proscribed are nearly opposites.

entries.meaning: Telling people exactly what they must do, instead of leaving it open. ---
examples: The guidelines are advisory, not prescriptive.
He takes a prescriptive view of grammar.
The new rules are much more prescriptive than the old ones.
entries.contrast: In language study, a prescriptive rule says how people ought to speak; a descriptive one records how they really do.

entries.meaning: Existing now, as opposed to in the past. ---
examples: Present-day Istanbul sits on top of the old city.
Present-day readers find the book slow.
The map shows the site in present-day Poland.
entries.contrast: Only before a noun. After a verb use current or modern: not The border is present-day.

entries.meaning: Clean and tidy enough to be seen by other people. ---
examples: Give me ten minutes to make myself presentable.
The apartment is finally presentable enough for guests.
He put on a presentable shirt for the interview.

entries.meaning: Preserved has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The town has a beautifully preserved main street.
The body was remarkably well preserved.
Preserved lemons are used in Moroccan cooking.
The jars of preserved peaches lasted all winter.

senses.head: Kept in good condition and not damaged by time
examples: The town has a beautifully preserved main street.
The body was remarkably well preserved.

senses.head: Treated so that it will not go bad, said of food
examples: Preserved lemons are used in Moroccan cooking.
The jars of preserved peaches lasted all winter.

entries.position: both — before a noun it usually carries an adverb: a well-preserved building
entries.comparison: not gradable — but graded with adverbs: well preserved, perfectly preserved

entries.meaning: Set to a value in advance, before you start using it. ---
examples: The oven has a preset temperature for bread.
The alarm goes off at a preset time.
The volume comes preset at fifty percent.
entries.form: pre- + set; set does not change in the past participle
entries.contrast: Preset is also a noun (save it as a preset) and a verb (preset the timer), with the stress moving to the first syllable in the noun.

entries.meaning: Presidential has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The presidential election is in November.
He's running a presidential campaign on a small budget.
He didn't sound very presidential in the debate.
She wanted a more presidential look for the photo.

senses.head: Relating to a president or to the office of president
examples: The presidential election is in November.
He's running a presidential campaign on a small budget.

senses.head: Dignified and impressive, the way a president is supposed to seem
examples: He didn't sound very presidential in the debate.
She wanted a more presidential look for the photo.

entries.position: both — the of the president sense only before a noun

entries.meaning: Pressed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'm a little pressed for time — can we talk tomorrow?
Families are pressed for cash after the holidays.
He wore a freshly pressed white shirt.
She keeps pressed flowers in an old book.

senses.head: Not having enough of something, especially time or money
examples: I'm a little pressed for time — can we talk tomorrow?
Families are pressed for cash after the holidays.

senses.head: Made flat and smooth by pressure or by an iron
examples: He wore a freshly pressed white shirt.
She keeps pressed flowers in an old book.

entries.русский: стеснённый (во времени, в деньгах); выглаженный, спрессованный
entries.position: both — the short of sense only after a verb
entries.takes: for + noun, in pressed for time, pressed for cash
entries.contrast: Hard-pressed is a set compound meaning 'having real difficulty': You'd be hard-pressed to find a better deal.

entries.meaning: Needing to be dealt with right away. ---
examples: We have more pressing problems right now.
There's a pressing need for more nurses.
Nothing is so pressing that it can't wait an hour.
entries.contrast: It goes with need, problem, issue, question, engagement — for an urgent message or package, say urgent.

entries.meaning: Widely admired and respected, so that being part of it raises your standing. ---
examples: She won a prestigious fellowship.
It's one of the most prestigious law schools in the country.
The award is prestigious but pays nothing.

entries.meaning: Doing or assuming more than you have the right to. ---
examples: It would be presumptuous of me to give her advice.
Don't be presumptuous — ask before you sit down.
He made the presumptuous assumption that we would pay.
entries.contrast: Spelled -tuous, not presumptious — a very common misspelling. It is not the same as pretentious: presumptuous is taking a liberty, pretentious is showing off.

entries.meaning: Aged roughly nine to twelve, just before the teenage years. ---
examples: The store sells clothes for preteen girls.
He has two preteen sons.
Preteen kids are the target audience.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a child of that age: a movie aimed at preteens.

entries.meaning: Not real, imagined as part of a game. ---
examples: They were having a pretend tea party.
He shot me with a pretend gun made of blocks.
She paid with pretend money from the board game.
entries.contrast: Children's word. The neutral adult choices are fake, toy or imaginary. Pretend is far more common as a verb: He pretended to be asleep.

entries.meaning: Trying to seem more important, cultured or clever than you really are. ---
examples: The restaurant is good but a little pretentious.
He uses long words to sound smart, which just seems pretentious.
It's the most pretentious movie I've seen all year.
entries.contrast: Always an insult in English. Keep it apart from presumptuous, which is about taking liberties rather than showing off.

entries.meaning: Beyond what is normal or natural, in a way that is hard to explain. ---
examples: She has a preternatural calm in a crisis.
He showed a preternatural talent for numbers.
The stillness in the room was preternatural.
entries.contrast: Formal and literary; in speech Americans say uncanny or unnatural.

entries.meaning: Prevailing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The prevailing view is that rates will fall.
She pays the prevailing wage for the area.
The prevailing winds come from the west.
Smoke drifted east with the prevailing wind.

senses.head: Most common or most widely accepted at the time
examples: The prevailing view is that rates will fall.
She pays the prevailing wage for the area.

senses.head: Blowing from one direction most of the time, said of wind
examples: The prevailing winds come from the west.
Smoke drifted east with the prevailing wind.

entries.meaning: Common in a place or among a group at a particular time. ---
examples: The disease is most prevalent among older men.
Cheating is more prevalent than teachers think.
It's a prevalent belief in the industry.
entries.contrast: Prevalent means common and widespread; prevailing means the one that dominates right now.

entries.meaning: Able to be stopped from happening. ---
examples: Most of these deaths are preventable.
It was a preventable accident.
Nearly every case was preventable with a vaccine.
entries.comparison: not gradable — but often graded with an adverb: largely preventable, entirely preventable

entries.meaning: Meant to stop illness or trouble before it starts. ---
examples: Insurance covers preventive care.
The dentist talked about preventive measures.
Preventive medicine saves money later.
entries.contrast: Preventative is also correct and widely used; preventive is the shorter form most American editors prefer.

entries.meaning: Coming before the present one in time or order. ---
examples: The previous owner painted everything beige.
I know her from a previous job.
See the previous chapter for the details.
entries.takes: to + noun, in the formal phrase previous to
entries.contrast: Only before a noun: not The job was previous. It means 'the one before this one' — for 'at an earlier time' use before or earlier.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the time before a war, usually the Second World War. ---
examples: They live in a prewar apartment building.
Prewar Vienna was a center of music.
The whole block is prewar.

entries.meaning: Priceless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The museum lost a priceless painting.
Her advice that year was priceless.
The look on his face was priceless.
His story about the airport is priceless.

senses.head: So valuable that no price could be put on it
examples: The museum lost a priceless painting.
Her advice that year was priceless.

senses.head: Informal: extremely funny
examples: The look on his face was priceless.
His story about the airport is priceless.

entries.comparison: not gradable — it is already an extreme
entries.contrast: Priceless does not mean 'worth nothing' — that is worthless. The -less here means 'too valuable to put a price on'.

entries.meaning: Costing more than you think it should. ---
examples: That neighborhood is getting pricey.
It's a pricey restaurant, but the food is worth it.
Tickets are pricier than they were last year.
entries.form: -y from price; the y becomes i before -er and -est
entries.contrast: Informal and a little softer than expensive. It is also spelled pricy, but pricey is the usual American spelling.

entries.meaning: Prickly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bush is prickly, so wear gloves.
The wool sweater felt prickly against my neck.
He gets prickly when you ask about money.
Money is a prickly subject in that family.
She's pricklier than usual today.

senses.head: Covered with sharp points, or giving a stinging feeling on the skin
examples: The bush is prickly, so wear gloves.
The wool sweater felt prickly against my neck.

senses.head: Easily annoyed, or easy to cause an argument about
examples: He gets prickly when you ask about money.
Money is a prickly subject in that family.
She's pricklier than usual today.

entries.form: -ly from prickle — an adjective, not an adverb
entries.contrast: It ends in -ly but it is an adjective: a prickly bush, He sounds prickly. There is no adverb pricklily.

entries.meaning: Costing more than you think it should. ---
examples: The hotel was pricy for what we got.
Parking downtown is pricy on game days.
Organic produce is pricier here than it is uptown.
entries.form: -y from price, with the silent e dropped
entries.contrast: The same word as pricey, which is the more common American spelling. Both make pricier, priciest.

entries.meaning: Very correct and formal in behavior, and easily shocked. ---
examples: She sat prim and straight on the edge of the chair.
He's a prim little man in a bow tie.
Her sister is even primmer about swearing than she is.
entries.contrast: The set phrase prim and proper means very correct and easily shocked.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the deepest, oldest part of human nature. ---
examples: He let out a primal scream.
There's a primal urge to protect your kids.
The fear of the dark is something primal.
entries.contrast: Primal is about deep, first instincts; primary means first in order or most important.

entries.meaning: Primary has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Our primary concern is the safety of the passengers.
The primary cause of the accident was ice on the road.
Reading is her primary way of relaxing.
See your primary care doctor before you see a specialist.
The disease is easy to treat in its primary stage.
Kids learn the primary colors first.
The painting uses nothing but primary colors.

senses.head: Most important; coming first in importance
examples: Our primary concern is the safety of the passengers.
The primary cause of the accident was ice on the road.
Reading is her primary way of relaxing.

senses.head: First in a series; at the earliest stage
examples: See your primary care doctor before you see a specialist.
The disease is easy to treat in its primary stage.

senses.head: Of the colors red, yellow and blue, from which all the others are mixed
examples: Kids learn the primary colors first.
The painting uses nothing but primary colors.
