entries.position: both — nearly always before a noun
entries.contrast: In the US primary is also a noun: the New Hampshire primary is the election that picks a party's candidate.

entries.meaning: Prime has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The butcher sells prime beef.
They bought a house in a prime location.
This is prime farmland.
He is the prime suspect in the case.
Cost was the prime consideration.
She's a prime example of what hard work can do.

senses.head: Of the best possible quality
examples: The butcher sells prime beef.
They bought a house in a prime location.
This is prime farmland.

senses.head: Main; most important or clearest
examples: He is the prime suspect in the case.
Cost was the prime consideration.
She's a prime example of what hard work can do.

entries.position: both — almost always before a noun
entries.contrast: Prime time is the evening viewing hours on TV, and a prime number is a math term; prime is also a noun: past his prime.

entries.meaning: Primitive has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The cabin was primitive — no electricity, no running water.
They cut the wood with primitive tools.
Our first computers look primitive now.
Primitive humans painted on cave walls.
The fossils come from primitive sea creatures.
Fear of the dark is a primitive feeling.
There was something primitive about the way the crowd screamed.

senses.head: Very simple and undeveloped; made without modern methods
examples: The cabin was primitive — no electricity, no running water.
They cut the wood with primitive tools.
Our first computers look primitive now.

senses.head: Belonging to a very early stage of human history or of life on earth
examples: Primitive humans painted on cave walls.
The fossils come from primitive sea creatures.

senses.head: Coming from instinct rather than from thought
examples: Fear of the dark is a primitive feeling.
There was something primitive about the way the crowd screamed.

entries.contrast: Calling living people primitive is offensive in English — say traditional, or name the culture.

entries.meaning: Primordial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Life began in a primordial soup of chemicals.
The valley floor looks primordial, untouched by anyone.
He felt a primordial fear when the lights went out.
There is a primordial pleasure in sitting by a fire.

senses.head: Existing from the very beginning of the world
examples: Life began in a primordial soup of chemicals.
The valley floor looks primordial, untouched by anyone.

senses.head: Very basic and deeply felt, as if it came from the beginning of time
examples: He felt a primordial fear when the lights went out.
There is a primordial pleasure in sitting by a fire.

entries.meaning: Acting on strong moral beliefs, even when that is not easy. ---
examples: She is a principled woman who says what she thinks.
He took a principled stand against the new policy.
Their refusal was principled, not political.
entries.contrast: Principled comes from principle (a moral rule); principal means main or the head of a school.

entries.meaning: Happening or existing before something else. ---
examples: You need prior experience for this job.
I'm sorry, I have a prior engagement that evening.
He has two prior convictions.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun; after a verb use earlier
entries.takes: to — in the phrase prior to + noun or -ing
entries.contrast: Prior to is a formal way of saying before: Prior to 1990, the town had no hospital.

entries.meaning: Too concerned with being proper, neat or polite. ---
examples: Don't be so prissy — it's only mud.
He has a prissy way of holding his fork.
She got prissier the older she got.

entries.meaning: Pristine has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The car is twenty years old but in pristine condition.
He keeps his kitchen pristine.
They hiked for three days through pristine wilderness.
The lake was pristine until the mill opened.

senses.head: Perfectly clean and looking like new
examples: The car is twenty years old but in pristine condition.
He keeps his kitchen pristine.

senses.head: Not spoiled or changed by people
examples: They hiked for three days through pristine wilderness.
The lake was pristine until the mill opened.

entries.meaning: Private has 3 distinct senses.
examples: This is a private conversation.
The beach in front of the hotel is private.
They ate in a private room at the back.
Their kids go to a private school.
He left the agency to work in the private sector.
My father was a very private man.
She is private about her health.

senses.head: For one person or group only, not for everyone
examples: This is a private conversation.
The beach in front of the hotel is private.
They ate in a private room at the back.

senses.head: Owned or run by a person or company, not by the government
examples: Their kids go to a private school.
He left the agency to work in the private sector.

senses.head: Not liking to talk about your own feelings or life
examples: My father was a very private man.
She is private about her health.

entries.contrast: In the US a private school is one you pay for and a public school is a free government school — the British use public school for the expensive kind.

entries.meaning: Allowed to know about something secret. ---
examples: Only three people were privy to the plan.
I wasn't privy to that conversation.
She was privy to information the rest of us never saw.
entries.position: predicative only — in be privy to
entries.contrast: Privy is also an old noun for an outdoor toilet.

entries.meaning: Having won a prize. ---
examples: She is a prizewinning journalist.
He grows prizewinning roses.
The museum bought a prizewinning photograph.
entries.contrast: Also spelled prize-winning; both are normal in American English.

entries.meaning: Done for free, especially legal work for people who cannot pay. ---
examples: The firm takes on several pro bono cases a year.
Her work with refugee families is pro bono.
He does pro bono work every Friday afternoon.
entries.form: from Latin pro bono publico — for the public good
entries.contrast: Pro bono is also an adverb: She represented the family pro bono.

entries.meaning: Believing that a woman should have the legal right to an abortion. ---
examples: She ran as a pro-choice candidate.
Most of his friends are pro-choice.
The magazine took a pro-choice position.

entries.meaning: Opposed to abortion being legal. ---
examples: The senator is pro-life.
They joined a pro-life march in Washington.
The group funds pro-life candidates in close races.

entries.meaning: Acting before a problem happens instead of waiting for it. ---
examples: We need a proactive approach to security.
Be proactive about your health.
The new manager is far more proactive than the last one.

entries.meaning: Likely to happen or likely to be true. ---
examples: Rain is probable tomorrow afternoon.
It is probable that the meeting will be canceled.
The probable cause of death was a heart attack.
entries.contrast: Probable is stronger than possible: a possible outcome could happen, a probable one most likely will.

entries.meaning: Belonging to a trial period, when someone can still be dismissed. ---
examples: New hires serve a ninety-day probationary period.
He is still a probationary member of the union.
She was hired on a probationary basis.

entries.meaning: Trying hard to find out the truth; searching. ---
examples: The reporter asked a few probing questions.
He gave me a probing look.
The book is a probing study of city finances.

entries.meaning: Problematic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The timing is problematic.
Getting everyone there by noon could be problematic.
The deal has a problematic history.
Several jokes in the old show now look problematic.
His comments about women were deeply problematic.

senses.head: Causing difficulty; full of problems
examples: The timing is problematic.
Getting everyone there by noon could be problematic.
The deal has a problematic history.

senses.head: Likely to offend people; morally questionable
examples: Several jokes in the old show now look problematic.
His comments about women were deeply problematic.

entries.meaning: Relating to the correct way of doing something, especially in law or an organization. ---
examples: The case was thrown out on a procedural error.
These are procedural questions, not questions of guilt.
The delay was purely procedural.

entries.meaning: Treated or changed in a factory, especially of food. ---
examples: Try to eat less processed food.
Processed cheese melts smoothly but tastes like nothing.
White bread is more processed than whole wheat.

entries.meaning: Prodigal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was prodigal with his father's money.
Years of prodigal spending left the company broke.
The prodigal son came back after ten years.
Chicago welcomed its prodigal quarterback home.

senses.head: Spending money in a wasteful way
examples: He was prodigal with his father's money.
Years of prodigal spending left the company broke.

senses.head: Coming home after leaving and living badly, like the son in the Bible story
examples: The prodigal son came back after ten years.
Chicago welcomed its prodigal quarterback home.

entries.meaning: Very large or very impressive in amount or ability. ---
examples: She has a prodigious memory for names.
The band produced a prodigious amount of music in three years.
He eats a prodigious amount for such a small guy.

entries.meaning: Productive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'm most productive in the morning.
The plant is more productive than it was a year ago.
She had a very productive week.
We had a productive conversation with the landlord.
The meeting wasn't productive at all.

senses.head: Getting a lot done; producing a lot
examples: I'm most productive in the morning.
The plant is more productive than it was a year ago.
She had a very productive week.

senses.head: Leading to a useful result
examples: We had a productive conversation with the landlord.
The meeting wasn't productive at all.

entries.meaning: Profane has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The coach's language was profane.
He shouted something profane at the referee.
The song was pulled for its profane lyrics.
The exhibit divides the art into sacred and profane.
He wrote both sacred and profane music.

senses.head: Using swear words, or showing no respect for religion
examples: The coach's language was profane.
He shouted something profane at the referee.
The song was pulled for its profane lyrics.

senses.head: Not religious; belonging to ordinary life
examples: The exhibit divides the art into sacred and profane.
He wrote both sacred and profane music.

entries.meaning: Stated openly by the person, often with a hint that it may not be the whole truth. ---
examples: He is a professed admirer of her work.
Her professed reason for leaving was the weather.
The group's professed aim is to help farmers.

entries.meaning: Professional has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He played professional baseball for six years.
She turned professional at nineteen.
The company pays for professional development.
It was a professional decision, not a personal one.
The repair looks very professional.
Please keep your tone professional.

senses.head: Done as a paid job rather than as a hobby
examples: He played professional baseball for six years.
She turned professional at nineteen.

senses.head: Relating to a job that requires training and a degree
examples: The company pays for professional development.
It was a professional decision, not a personal one.

senses.head: Showing the skill and the behavior expected at work
examples: The repair looks very professional.
Please keep your tone professional.

entries.opposite: amateur; in the third sense unprofessional
entries.contrast: Professional is also a noun: a young professional.

entries.meaning: Able to do something well because of training and practice. ---
examples: She is proficient in Spanish and Portuguese.
You have to be proficient at reading music.
After a month he was a proficient driver.

entries.meaning: Profitable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The store finally became profitable last year.
Coffee is the most profitable item on the menu.
It was a profitable afternoon in the library.
We had a profitable exchange of ideas.

senses.head: Making money
examples: The store finally became profitable last year.
Coffee is the most profitable item on the menu.

senses.head: Useful; producing a good result
examples: It was a profitable afternoon in the library.
We had a profitable exchange of ideas.

entries.meaning: Wasting money or resources in a shocking way. ---
examples: The report criticizes the profligate use of water.
He was profligate with other people's money.
Years of profligate spending caught up with the city.

entries.meaning: Profound has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The accident had a profound effect on her.
He felt a profound sense of relief.
The child was born with profound hearing loss.
It's a profound book about grief.
His answer was simple but profound.

senses.head: Very great or very strong
examples: The accident had a profound effect on her.
He felt a profound sense of relief.
The child was born with profound hearing loss.

senses.head: Showing deep understanding and serious thought
examples: It's a profound book about grief.
His answer was simple but profound.

entries.contrast: Profound is not used for physical depth — a lake is deep, never profound.

entries.meaning: Produced or given in very large amounts. ---
examples: He offered profuse apologies for being late.
Profuse sweating is one symptom of the illness.
She was profuse in her thanks.

entries.meaning: Progressive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is one of the most progressive members of the city council.
The school has progressive ideas about homework.
MS is a progressive disease.
We have a progressive tax system, so higher earners pay a higher rate.

senses.head: Favoring social change and new ideas
examples: She is one of the most progressive members of the city council.
The school has progressive ideas about homework.

senses.head: Happening gradually, in stages
examples: MS is a progressive disease.
We have a progressive tax system, so higher earners pay a higher rate.

entries.contrast: In grammar the progressive is the -ing form: is working, was working.

entries.meaning: Not allowed by a law or a rule. ---
examples: Smoking is prohibited in all federal buildings.
Cameras are prohibited inside the theater.
Prohibited items are listed on the airline's website.
entries.takes: from + -ing, of a person: He is prohibited from driving

entries.meaning: Prohibitive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cost of the repairs was prohibitive.
Prohibitive rents are pushing families out of the city.
The state passed prohibitive legislation on fireworks.
Prohibitive tariffs killed the trade.

senses.head: So expensive that you cannot afford it
examples: The cost of the repairs was prohibitive.
Prohibitive rents are pushing families out of the city.

senses.head: Meant to stop something by law
examples: The state passed prohibitive legislation on fireworks.
Prohibitive tariffs killed the trade.

entries.meaning: Calculated in advance for some future time. ---
examples: The projected cost of the bridge is four billion dollars.
Projected sales for next year look strong.
The projected finish date keeps moving.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the working class, especially in Marxist writing. ---
examples: The poster uses proletarian imagery.
He teaches a course on proletarian literature of the 1930s.
The party claimed to speak for the proletarian masses.
entries.contrast: Proletarian is also a noun for a member of the working class.

entries.meaning: Prolific has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was a prolific songwriter.
She is one of the most prolific scorers in the league.
Rabbits are prolific breeders.
The vine is prolific in warm weather.

senses.head: Producing a great deal of work
examples: He was a prolific songwriter.
She is one of the most prolific scorers in the league.

senses.head: Producing a lot of young or fruit; growing in large numbers
examples: Rabbits are prolific breeders.
The vine is prolific in warm weather.

entries.meaning: Continuing for a long time, usually longer than is good. ---
examples: Prolonged exposure to the sun damages your skin.
After a prolonged illness, he went back to work.
There was a prolonged silence on the other end of the line.

entries.meaning: Prominent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is a prominent civil rights attorney.
The paper gave the story a prominent place on page one.
He has a prominent chin.
The sign is prominent enough to read from the road.

senses.head: Important and well known
examples: She is a prominent civil rights attorney.
The paper gave the story a prominent place on page one.

senses.head: Easy to see or notice, often because it sticks out
examples: He has a prominent chin.
The sign is prominent enough to read from the road.

entries.meaning: Having sex with many different people. ---
examples: He was accused of leading a promiscuous life.
She resented being called promiscuous.
Some birds are promiscuous, mating with several partners a season.
entries.contrast: In formal writing promiscuous can also mean mixed together with no care: a promiscuous pile of papers.

entries.meaning: Showing signs of being good or successful later. ---
examples: She's a promising young violinist.
The early results look promising.
It was the most promising lead the detectives had.

entries.meaning: Used to advertise a product or an event. ---
examples: They sent out promotional emails all week.
The band is on a promotional tour.
Free samples and other promotional items filled the booth.

entries.meaning: Prompt has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Thank you for your prompt reply.
Prompt treatment saved his leg.
Please be prompt — the bus leaves at six.
She is always prompt with her payments.

senses.head: Done without delay
examples: Thank you for your prompt reply.
Prompt treatment saved his leg.

senses.head: Arriving or acting at the arranged time
examples: Please be prompt — the bus leaves at six.
She is always prompt with her payments.

entries.contrast: Prompt is also a verb (What prompted the change?) and a noun (a writing prompt); the adverb is promptly.

entries.meaning: Very noticeable or strong. ---
examples: He walks with a pronounced limp.
She has a pronounced Southern accent.
The difference is more pronounced in older patients.
entries.contrast: This adjective has nothing to do with saying words — He pronounced my name wrong is the verb.

entries.meaning: Correctly describing what will happen later. ---
examples: His warning about the flood turned out to be prophetic.
The last chapter of the novel feels prophetic today.
She wrote a prophetic essay about the collapse of the industry.

entries.meaning: Likely to lead to a good result; favorable. ---
examples: It was not a propitious time to ask for a raise.
The weather was propitious for sailing.
They waited for a more propitious moment.

entries.meaning: Changing in size or amount at the same rate as something else. ---
examples: The fine is proportional to your income.
Pressure is proportional to depth.
Each state gets a proportional share of the money.
entries.contrast: Proportional representation gives a party seats in proportion to the votes it won.

entries.meaning: In the right relation in size or degree to something else. ---
examples: The punishment should be proportionate to the crime.
Their response was hardly proportionate.
Each partner puts in a proportionate share of the costs.
entries.contrast: Proportional is the mathematical word (proportional to speed); proportionate usually says that something is fair.

entries.meaning: Proprietary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The software uses a proprietary file format.
The recipe is proprietary, so they won't share it.
He put a proprietary hand on the back of her chair.
She is very proprietary about her desk.

senses.head: Owned by a company and protected by a patent or a trademark
examples: The software uses a proprietary file format.
The recipe is proprietary, so they won't share it.

senses.head: Behaving as if you owned someone or something
examples: He put a proprietary hand on the back of her chair.
She is very proprietary about her desk.

entries.comparison: not gradable — but the attitude sense takes very

entries.meaning: Ordinary and dull; showing no imagination. ---
examples: The truth was more prosaic: he had simply forgotten.
It's a prosaic little town with one movie theater.
Her writing is clear but prosaic.

entries.meaning: Rich and successful. ---
examples: The town was prosperous while the mill was open.
They come from a prosperous farming family.
The 1990s were the country's most prosperous years.

entries.meaning: Being an artificial part that replaces a missing part of the body. ---
examples: He runs on a prosthetic leg.
The clinic fits prosthetic limbs for veterans.
The actor wore a prosthetic nose.

entries.meaning: Prostrate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The worshippers lay prostrate before the altar.
We found him prostrate on the kitchen floor.
She was prostrate with grief for weeks.
The whole team was prostrate after the race.

senses.head: Lying flat on the ground, face down
examples: The worshippers lay prostrate before the altar.
We found him prostrate on the kitchen floor.

senses.head: Completely overcome by grief, illness or exhaustion
examples: She was prostrate with grief for weeks.
The whole team was prostrate after the race.

entries.takes: with + noun, in the second sense
entries.contrast: Do not confuse prostrate with prostate, the gland — one r is the whole difference.

entries.meaning: Protected has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The harbor is protected from the wind.
Children in that neighborhood feel protected.
Sea turtles are a protected species.
The wetland is a protected area.

senses.head: Kept safe from harm or damage
examples: The harbor is protected from the wind.
Children in that neighborhood feel protected.

senses.head: Guarded by law
examples: Sea turtles are a protected species.
The wetland is a protected area.

entries.meaning: Protective has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He is very protective of his little sister.
The dog gets protective when strangers come near.
Wear protective gloves for this part.
The phone came with a protective case.

senses.head: Wanting to keep someone safe
examples: He is very protective of his little sister.
The dog gets protective when strangers come near.

senses.head: Made or worn to protect something
examples: Wear protective gloves for this part.
The phone came with a protective case.

entries.takes: of + noun, in the first sense

entries.meaning: Being the first or the clearest example of a type. ---
examples: He is the prototypical small-town lawyer.
The song is a prototypical early rock ballad.
She played the prototypical tough detective.

entries.meaning: Lasting much longer than expected or wanted. ---
examples: The company faces a protracted legal battle.
After a protracted strike, the two sides finally agreed.
It was a protracted and painful divorce.

entries.meaning: Sticking out beyond a surface. ---
examples: A protruding nail tore my sleeve.
The baby had big protruding ears.
Watch the protruding edge of that shelf.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun; after a verb use the verb protrude or stick out

entries.meaning: Shown by evidence or experience to be true or to work. ---
examples: She has a proven track record in sales.
This is a proven method for learning vocabulary.
Nothing has been proven yet.
entries.contrast: As the past participle of prove, Americans say either proved or proven (It has proved useful), but before a noun only proven works: a proven method.

entries.meaning: Proverbial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We were looking for the proverbial needle in a haystack.
He's the proverbial bull in a china shop.
Her proverbial patience finally ran out.
The town's proverbial friendliness is real.

senses.head: Used to show that you are quoting a well-known saying
examples: We were looking for the proverbial needle in a haystack.
He's the proverbial bull in a china shop.

senses.head: So well known that everyone talks about it
examples: Her proverbial patience finally ran out.
The town's proverbial friendliness is real.

entries.meaning: Provincial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His views on food are hopelessly provincial.
I found the town warm but provincial.
She grew up in a quiet provincial city.
The provincial government in Ontario runs the schools.

senses.head: Narrow in outlook, with little experience of the wider world
examples: His views on food are hopelessly provincial.
I found the town warm but provincial.

senses.head: Belonging to the parts of a country away from the capital, or to a province
examples: She grew up in a quiet provincial city.
The provincial government in Ontario runs the schools.

entries.meaning: Arranged for now and likely to be changed later. ---
examples: We've set a provisional date of May 3.
The agreement is provisional until the board votes.
He was given a provisional license.

entries.meaning: Provocative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She asked a deliberately provocative question.
The article is provocative but well argued.
The dress was too provocative for the office.
He gave her a provocative smile.

senses.head: Meant to make people angry, or to make them think hard
examples: She asked a deliberately provocative question.
The article is provocative but well argued.

senses.head: Meant to attract sexual interest
examples: The dress was too provocative for the office.
He gave her a provocative smile.

entries.meaning: Careful and sensible about risks and money. ---
examples: It would be prudent to save some of that bonus.
She made a few prudent investments.
A prudent driver slows down in the rain.
entries.takes: to-infinitive — It would be prudent to wait

entries.meaning: Easily shocked by anything to do with sex or the body. ---
examples: My grandmother was prudish about swimsuits.
The network's old rules look prudish today.
Don't be prudish — it's a medical exam.

entries.meaning: Having or causing too much interest in sex, especially other people's. ---
examples: The coverage appealed to prurient curiosity.
The judge said the film had no prurient appeal.
His interest in the case felt prurient.

entries.meaning: Of Prussia, the German state that led the founding of Germany in 1871. ---
examples: The museum has a collection of Prussian uniforms.
His grandfather came from a Prussian family.
Prussian blue is a deep, dark blue.
entries.contrast: Prussian is also a noun for a person from Prussia; do not read it as Russian.

entries.meaning: Too interested in other people's private business. ---
examples: They put up a fence to keep the yard safe from prying eyes.
He had a prying neighbor who watched every car.
She answered the prying questions as briefly as she could.
entries.русский: любопытный, сующий нос в чужие дела
entries.contrast: The verb pry also means to force something open: He pried the lid off.

entries.meaning: Pretending to be science but not based on real evidence. ---
examples: The book is full of pseudoscientific claims about vitamins.
Astrology is pseudoscientific.
He dresses old prejudices in pseudoscientific language.
entries.form: pseudo- + scientific; the first p is silent

entries.meaning: Psychedelic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Doctors are studying psychedelic drugs as a treatment for depression.
He wrote about his first psychedelic experience.
She wore a psychedelic shirt.
The poster is psychedelic, all orange and purple swirls.

senses.head: Causing hallucinations, as LSD or certain mushrooms do
examples: Doctors are studying psychedelic drugs as a treatment for depression.
He wrote about his first psychedelic experience.

senses.head: Having bright swirling colors and patterns, like the art of the 1960s
examples: She wore a psychedelic shirt.
The poster is psychedelic, all orange and purple swirls.

entries.meaning: Relating to mental illness and its treatment. ---
examples: He spent two weeks in a psychiatric hospital.
She needs a full psychiatric evaluation.
The jail offers almost no psychiatric care.

entries.meaning: Psychic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She claims to have psychic powers.
How did you know that? Are you psychic?
The war left deep psychic wounds.
He writes about psychic energy.

senses.head: Able to know things by supernatural means
examples: She claims to have psychic powers.
How did you know that? Are you psychic?

senses.head: Of the mind rather than the body
examples: The war left deep psychic wounds.
He writes about psychic energy.

entries.contrast: Psychic is also a noun: She went to a psychic.

entries.meaning: Affecting the mind or the mood, as a drug does. ---
examples: Caffeine is the most widely used psychoactive substance in the world.
The law covers all psychoactive drugs.
Some of these plants are mildly psychoactive.

entries.meaning: Relating to psychoanalysis, the therapy built on Freud's ideas. ---
examples: She trained as a psychoanalytic therapist.
The essay offers a psychoanalytic reading of the novel.
He belongs to a psychoanalytic institute in New York.

entries.meaning: Psychological has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The crash left psychological scars as well as broken bones.
She got psychological help after the attack.
The doctor said the pain was psychological.
His block about swimming is purely psychological.

senses.head: Relating to the mind and the way it works
examples: The crash left psychological scars as well as broken bones.
She got psychological help after the attack.

senses.head: Caused by the mind rather than by the body
examples: The doctor said the pain was psychological.
His block about swimming is purely psychological.

entries.meaning: Having or showing no conscience and no feeling for other people. ---
examples: The movie gave us one more psychopathic killer.
He studies psychopathic behavior in children.
Her ex was charming and, she now thinks, psychopathic.

entries.meaning: Of a physical illness that is caused or made worse by worry and stress. ---
examples: The headaches turned out to be psychosomatic.
He studies psychosomatic illness.
Calling a symptom psychosomatic does not mean the person is faking.

entries.meaning: Suffering from or showing a mental illness in which a person loses touch with reality. ---
examples: He had a psychotic episode and was hospitalized.
The patient became psychotic after days without sleep.
Psychotic symptoms include hearing voices.
entries.contrast: Psychotic (losing touch with reality) is not the same as psychopathic (having no conscience), though movies mix the two up.

entries.meaning: Of a drug that changes mood, thinking or behavior. ---
examples: The nursing home hands out too many psychotropic medications.
Psychotropic drugs have to be prescribed by a doctor.
She studies the effect of psychotropic substances on sleep.

entries.meaning: Of the area at the lower front of the body, where the legs join. ---
examples: The doctor examined the pubic area.
Pubic hair grows during puberty.
He fractured his pubic bone in the fall.
entries.contrast: Pubic and public differ by one letter and mean completely different things — check what you have typed.

entries.meaning: Public has 3 distinct senses.
examples: We met in a public park.
The library is a public building.
Their kids go to public school.
The city needs better public transportation.
His resignation became public on Friday.
She made a public apology.

senses.head: Open to everyone; for the use of all people
examples: We met in a public park.
The library is a public building.

senses.head: Paid for and run by the government
examples: Their kids go to public school.
The city needs better public transportation.

senses.head: Known to everyone; not secret
examples: His resignation became public on Friday.
She made a public apology.

entries.contrast: In the US a public school is a free government school; in Britain a public school is an expensive private one. The public is also a noun.

entries.meaning: Willing to do things for the good of the community. ---
examples: A few public-spirited neighbors cleaned up the empty lot.
It was a public-spirited thing to do.
He is one of the most public-spirited people in town.

entries.meaning: Made known to the public, especially through the media. ---
examples: The trial was widely publicized.
It was the most heavily publicized movie of the year.
Their engagement was never publicized.
entries.position: both — before a noun it usually comes with an adverb: a widely publicized trial

entries.meaning: Published has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The published study covers ten years of data.
Her letters were published after her death.
He is a published poet.
Being a published author changed nothing about her mornings.

senses.head: Printed or put online for people to read
examples: The published study covers ten years of data.
Her letters were published after her death.

senses.head: Of a writer whose work has come out in print
examples: He is a published poet.
Being a published author changed nothing about her mornings.

entries.meaning: A little fat, in a soft and often likable way. ---
examples: The baby has pudgy little fingers.
He was a pudgy kid who grew up tall and thin.
I'm pudgier now than I was in college.

entries.meaning: Silly and childish in a way that annoys people. ---
examples: His jokes are puerile.
The debate sank into a puerile argument about names.
I expected better than this puerile nonsense.

entries.meaning: Puffy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My eyes are puffy from crying.
Her ankle looked puffier than it did yesterday.
Puffy white clouds sat over the valley.
He wore a puffy down jacket.

senses.head: Swollen, especially around the eyes or the face
examples: My eyes are puffy from crying.
Her ankle looked puffier than it did yesterday.

senses.head: Soft, rounded and full of air
examples: Puffy white clouds sat over the valley.
He wore a puffy down jacket.

entries.meaning: Eager to argue or to fight. ---
examples: The candidate was pugnacious in the debate.
He's a small, pugnacious man who never backs down.
Her tone turned pugnacious.

entries.meaning: Of the lungs. ---
examples: He died of a pulmonary embolism.
She has a chronic pulmonary disease.
The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs.

entries.meaning: Informal: excited and full of energy. ---
examples: I'm so pumped about the trip.
The whole team was pumped before the game.
Somehow he gets pumped for every Monday meeting.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: I'm pumped
entries.contrast: Often pumped up, which can also describe muscles right after a workout.

entries.meaning: Punch-drunk has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The old fighter was punch-drunk by forty.
He moved like a punch-drunk boxer.
After three hours of meetings I felt punch-drunk.
The town is punch-drunk from one flood after another.

senses.head: Dazed and unsteady from being hit in the head too many times
examples: The old fighter was punch-drunk by forty.
He moved like a punch-drunk boxer.

senses.head: Confused and worn out by stress or by one blow after another
examples: After three hours of meetings I felt punch-drunk.
The town is punch-drunk from one flood after another.

entries.meaning: Very careful to do everything correctly and politely. ---
examples: He is punctilious about answering every email.
She kept punctilious records of every dollar.
His manners were punctilious, almost old-fashioned.

entries.meaning: Arriving or doing something at the arranged time. ---
examples: She is always punctual.
He's a punctual man who hates waiting.
The trains there have a reputation for being punctual.
entries.contrast: Punctual describes people and services; a package or a paper that arrives at the right time is on time, not punctual.

entries.meaning: With a small hole made through it. ---
examples: A punctured tire left us on the shoulder for an hour.
The X-ray showed a punctured lung.
The can was punctured and leaking.

entries.meaning: Pungent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kitchen filled with the pungent smell of garlic.
Blue cheese is too pungent for me.
She wrote a pungent review of the mayor's speech.
His comments are short and pungent.

senses.head: Having a strong, sharp smell or taste
examples: The kitchen filled with the pungent smell of garlic.
Blue cheese is too pungent for me.

senses.head: Sharp and direct, often funny or critical
examples: She wrote a pungent review of the mayor's speech.
His comments are short and pungent.

entries.meaning: That can be punished by law. ---
examples: Tax fraud is punishable by up to five years in prison.
It is a punishable offense in every state.
Under the old rules the same act was not punishable.
entries.takes: by + noun — punishable by a fine

entries.meaning: So hard or so fast that it exhausts you. ---
examples: She keeps a punishing schedule of concerts.
They set a punishing pace up the hill.
It was the most punishing winter in years.
entries.contrast: A punishing schedule is not a punishment — the word only says that it wears you out.

entries.meaning: Punitive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The jury awarded punitive damages.
The state took punitive action against the company.
The tax on imported steel is punitive.
Some landlords charge punitive late fees.

senses.head: Meant to punish someone
examples: The jury awarded punitive damages.
The state took punitive action against the company.

senses.head: So severe that it feels like a punishment
examples: The tax on imported steel is punitive.
Some landlords charge punitive late fees.

entries.meaning: Of punk rock and its loud, angry style of music, clothes and hair. ---
examples: They played in a punk band in high school.
She still wears her hair in a punk cut.
The store sells punk T-shirts and patches.
entries.contrast: Punk is mostly a noun — punk rock, or a punk meaning a young troublemaker.

entries.meaning: Puny has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was a puny kid who dreaded gym class.
The second batch of seedlings came up even punier than the first.
They offered a puny two percent raise.
Our marketing budget is puny compared to theirs.

senses.head: Small and weak
examples: He was a puny kid who dreaded gym class.
The second batch of seedlings came up even punier than the first.

senses.head: Too small to be worth much
examples: They offered a puny two percent raise.
Our marketing budget is puny compared to theirs.

entries.meaning: Pure has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The ring is pure gold.
Spring water out here is purer than anything from a tap.
It was pure luck that we found the keys.
That story is pure nonsense.
His motives were pure, whatever people said.
She had the purest heart of anyone in that family.

senses.head: Not mixed with anything else
examples: The ring is pure gold.
Spring water out here is purer than anything from a tap.

senses.head: Nothing but; complete — used before a noun to stress that something is only what it is
examples: It was pure luck that we found the keys.
That story is pure nonsense.

senses.head: Morally clean and innocent
examples: His motives were pure, whatever people said.
She had the purest heart of anyone in that family.

entries.position: both — the nothing but sense only before a noun: pure luck

entries.meaning: Of an animal: having parents of the same breed. ---
examples: They paid a lot for a purebred German shepherd.
Is your cat purebred or a rescue?
Purebred horses come with papers.

entries.meaning: Very strict about morals, especially about pleasure and sex. ---
examples: Her parents were puritanical about dating.
The town still has a puritanical streak.
He's more puritanical about alcohol than anyone I know.

entries.meaning: Slightly purple in color. ---
examples: The bruise turned a purplish color overnight.
The sky looked more purplish than pink just after sunset.
She wore a purplish gray sweater.

entries.meaning: Built specially for one particular use. ---
examples: The city opened a purpose-built shelter downtown.
The lab is purpose-built for testing engines.
They practice in a purpose-built training facility.

entries.meaning: Having a clear aim, and determined about it. ---
examples: She crossed the room with purposeful strides.
He seemed more purposeful after he changed jobs.
The work is hard, but it feels purposeful.
entries.contrast: Purposeful means having a clear aim. The adverb purposely means on purpose, and purposefully means with determination — He purposely broke it is not He purposefully broke it.

entries.meaning: Formal and legal: in accordance with a law, rule or agreement. ---
examples: The records were released pursuant to a court order.
Payments will be made pursuant to the terms of the contract.
The city acted pursuant to its emergency powers.
entries.position: after the noun — a notice pursuant to section 5
entries.contrast: Legal boilerplate, and almost always in the fixed phrase pursuant to. It never goes before a noun. In ordinary English say under or in accordance with.

entries.meaning: Trying so hard to get what you want that you annoy people. ---
examples: The salesman got pushy when we said no.
Some parents are pushier than others about grades.
I don't want to be pushy, but the deadline is Friday.

entries.meaning: Feeling that other people take advantage of you or give you too much to do. ---
examples: She let out a long, put-upon sigh.
He always sounds put-upon when you ask for help.
The nurses feel more put-upon than ever after months of extra shifts.
entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb put upon (to impose on someone)

entries.meaning: Generally believed to be what the noun says, though it is not proven. ---
examples: The putative father asked for a DNA test.
Police named a putative motive for the attack.
The putative leader of the group denies any role in it.
entries.contrast: Formal and mostly legal. In everyday English say alleged, supposed or so-called.

entries.meaning: Putrid has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A putrid smell was coming from the back of the fridge.
The water in the bottom of the cooler was putrid.
The team played a putrid first half.
His excuse was even more putrid than the last one.

senses.head: Rotting, and smelling terrible
examples: A putrid smell was coming from the back of the fridge.
The water in the bottom of the cooler was putrid.

senses.head: Informal: very bad indeed
examples: The team played a putrid first half.
His excuse was even more putrid than the last one.

entries.meaning: Relating to the Greek mathematician Pythagoras, especially to his theorem about right triangles.
examples: We used the Pythagorean theorem to find the third side.
Every geometry student memorizes the Pythagorean formula.
The Pythagorean school believed numbers ruled the universe.
entries.contrast: Always capitalized. Note the stress: pi-thag-uh-REE-uhn, not on the first syllable.
